cards.statement: `#[derive(Display)]` automatically supplies `{}` formatting for a struct.
cards.explanation: Rust's built-in derive supports Debug for {:?}. Display formatting with {} needs an implementation written by the programmer.
cards.misconception: Rust derives Display just as it derives Debug.

source.title: Derivable Traits - The Rust Programming Language

cards.statement: A derived `Clone` implementation preserves sharing through an `Arc<Mutex<T>>` field.
cards.explanation: Derived Clone calls clone on the struct's fields. Cloning an Arc<Mutex<T>> field retains a handle to the existing allocation, so the protected state remains shared.

cards.statement: When their block ends, Rust drops its remaining local variables in declaration order.
cards.explanation: At the end of a scope, Rust drops remaining local variables in reverse declaration order. Later declarations are cleaned up before earlier ones.
cards.misconception: Rust cleans up local variables in the order they were declared.

cards.statement: Calling `std::mem::drop(s)` disposes of the local `String` named `s` before its block ends.
cards.explanation: std::mem::drop gives an explicit point for a value's cleanup. The local's enclosing scope can continue after the String has been disposed of.

source.title: Running Code on Cleanup with the Drop Trait

cards.statement: When deriving `Default` for an enum, Rust automatically selects its first unit variant.
cards.explanation: Derived Default needs a #[default] marker on a unit variant; declaration order does not select the value. Default::default() returns the marked variant.
cards.misconception: Deriving Default chooses the earliest unit variant automatically.

cards.statement: A value of type `f64` satisfies an `Eq` trait bound on a generic function parameter.
cards.explanation: f64 implements PartialEq rather than Eq. NaN compares unequal to itself, so floating-point equality lacks Eq's reflexivity guarantee.
cards.misconception: Floating-point equality satisfies the same Eq contract as integer equality.

cards.statement: Deriving `PartialOrd` on a struct gives earlier declared fields priority during comparison.
cards.explanation: Derived PartialOrd compares fields lexicographically from top to bottom. Later fields matter after preceding field comparisons return equal.

cards.statement: The `Hash` contract requires equal keys to produce equal hashes under the same hashing setup.
cards.explanation: Hash implementations have to agree with key equality. HashMap and HashSet rely on that agreement when locating equal keys.

cards.statement: `impl From<Source> for Target` automatically enables `Source: Into<Target>`.
cards.explanation: The standard library's blanket implementation provides Into<Target> for Source when Target implements From<Source>. The conversion follows the same From implementation.

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `TryFrom` and `TryInto` are in scope through the standard prelude.
cards.explanation: Rust 2021's prelude imports TryFrom and TryInto for ordinary Rust code, making their trait methods available in scope.

source.title: Additions to the prelude - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: A `String` satisfies an `AsRef<Vec<u8>>` bound for code that reads its UTF-8 bytes.
cards.explanation: String implements AsRef<[u8]>, exposing its UTF-8 data as a borrowed byte slice. It does not implement AsRef<Vec<u8>>.
cards.misconception: String implements AsRef<Vec<u8>> to expose its byte storage.

cards.statement: Deref coercion converts an owned `Box<i32>` argument into the `i32` expected by a function.
cards.explanation: Rust applies Deref coercion to reference arguments. A function taking &i32 accepts &Box<i32>; an i32 parameter still expects a plain integer.
cards.misconception: Deref coercion extracts a smart pointer's owned value to satisfy a value parameter.

cards.statement: For an owned `String` named `text`, the closure `move || text.len()` implements `Fn`.
cards.explanation: The move keyword determines capture by value. This closure reads its captured String through a shared borrow, so its body satisfies Fn.

cards.statement: For an owned `String` named `text`, the closure `|| text` implements `FnMut`.
cards.explanation: Returning the captured String moves it out of the closure. The closure implements FnOnce, but its body prevents repeated calls through FnMut.
cards.misconception: A closure can implement FnMut while moving its captured String out on invocation.

cards.statement: `let f: fn(i32) -> i32 = |x| x + 1;` coerces the closure to a function pointer.
cards.explanation: This ordinary closure captures no environment values. Rust coerces it to a function pointer with the matching parameter and return types.

cards.statement: The supertrait chain makes an `F: FnOnce()` bound sufficient for an `F: Fn()` parameter.
cards.explanation: Fn requires FnMut, which in turn requires FnOnce. A type implementing Fn satisfies a FnOnce bound; a FnOnce bound alone gives no Fn guarantee.
cards.misconception: Closure trait supertraits imply that implementing FnOnce also implements Fn.

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `|| pair.0.len()` captures both fields of a local `(String, String)` tuple.
cards.explanation: Edition 2021 permits closures to capture individual fields. This closure captures the first tuple field, leaving the second outside its capture.
cards.misconception: Accessing one field in a closure captures the entire tuple in edition 2021.

source.title: Disjoint capture in closures - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: An iterator's `next()` call returns `Some(item)` when it yields an item.
cards.explanation: Iterator::next returns an Option: Some(item) contains a yielded item, while None signals that the call yields no item.

cards.statement: `iter.map(f)` immediately runs `f` over the iterator's remaining items.
cards.explanation: Iterator::map creates an adapter and calls f as that adapter yields items. Creating the adapter alone leaves those transformations unevaluated.
cards.misconception: Creating a map iterator eagerly invokes its closure over the input.

cards.statement: A `Vec<_>` result annotation tells `collect()` which container type to build.
cards.explanation: Iterator::collect uses the expected result type to select a collection. Vec<_> supplies the container type while Rust infers the element type.

cards.statement: The iterator from `iter()` on a `Vec<String>` yields borrowed `&String` items.
cards.explanation: Vec::iter produces shared references to elements in the vector. The iterator gives access to the existing strings through borrowing.

source.title: Processing a Series of Items with Iterators

cards.statement: In the 2021 edition, `.into_iter()` on a `[String; 2]` yields owned `String` values.
cards.explanation: The array method call uses the array's by-value IntoIterator implementation in edition 2021. Its items are owned elements from the array.

source.title: IntoIterator for arrays - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: In the 2024 edition, `b.into_iter()` borrows `b` when `b` has type `Box<[String]>`.
cards.explanation: In edition 2024, this method call consumes the boxed slice and returns an iterator over owned String values. The original box is moved.
cards.misconception: The boxed-slice into_iter method call keeps borrowing the box in edition 2024.

source.title: Add IntoIterator for Box<[T]> - The Rust Edition Guide

cards.statement: `collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()` keeps requesting items after the iterator yields `Err`.
cards.explanation: Collecting into Result stops at the first Err and returns that error. It leaves subsequent iterator items unrequested.
cards.misconception: Collecting Result items continues past an Err before choosing the returned error.

cards.statement: `Box::new(42_i32)` places the integer payload on the heap behind the resulting `Box<i32>` pointer.
cards.explanation: Box::new allocates the i32 on the heap. The Box value holds a pointer to that allocation.

source.title: Using Box<T> to Point to Data on the Heap

cards.statement: For `enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil }`, the compiler uses `Nil` to give `List` a finite size.
cards.explanation: A direct List field leaves the enum's layout recursively unbounded despite Nil. Replacing that field with Box<List> gives the recursive link a known size.
cards.misconception: A recursive enum's terminating variant also terminates compile-time layout recursion.

source.title: Using Box<T> to Point to Data on the Heap

cards.statement: A smart pointer implementing `Deref<Target = T>` lets `*pointer` access its target of type `T`.
cards.explanation: In an immutable context, *pointer uses *Deref::deref(&pointer). Deref::deref supplies the shared reference to the target.

cards.statement: A `Box<dyn std::fmt::Display>` value has a size known at compile time despite its unsized target.
cards.explanation: Pointers to trait objects have a fixed layout containing pointer information and metadata. The trait object they point to is dynamically sized.

source.title: Dynamically sized types - The Rust Reference

cards.statement: `Rc::clone(&value)` allocates a separate copy of the pointed-to `String` and its text buffer.
cards.explanation: Rc::clone creates another owner of the same allocation and increments its strong count. It leaves the pointed-to String and its text buffer shared.
cards.misconception: Cloning an Rc<String> duplicates the inner String rather than its ownership handle.

cards.statement: A mutable binding lets its owner change a shared `Rc<Vec<i32>>`'s elements through dereferencing.
cards.explanation: Rc dereferencing provides shared access even through a mut binding. Changing data shared by its owners needs interior mutability, such as an Rc<RefCell<Vec<i32>>>.
cards.misconception: Marking an Rc binding mut makes its shared pointee mutably accessible.

cards.statement: `std::rc::Weak::upgrade` returns an `Option<Rc<T>>` to account for the allocation's value expiring.
cards.explanation: Weak::upgrade returns Some(Rc<T>) when upgrading succeeds and None after the inner value has been dropped. A weak pointer leaves the value free to expire.

cards.statement: A strong `Rc<T>` reference cycle can leak its values while the program retains Rust's memory safety.
cards.explanation: Strong references around an Rc cycle keep its values allocated. Rust's memory safety guarantees permit memory leaks.

cards.statement: Calling `get` on a `Cell<i32>` can return a shared reference to the integer stored inside the cell.
cards.explanation: Cell<i32>::get returns an i32 copied from the cell's current value. Cell::get is available when the contained type implements Copy.
cards.misconception: Cell::get borrows its inner value and returns a shared reference.

cards.statement: The compiler resolves conflicts between `RefCell::borrow` and `RefCell::borrow_mut` during compilation.
cards.explanation: RefCell tracks its active borrows at run time. Its borrow and borrow_mut methods panic when the requested borrow conflicts with the active state.
cards.misconception: RefCell's borrow conflicts receive the same compile-time validation as ordinary references.

source.title: RefCell<T> and the Interior Mutability Pattern

cards.statement: `Cell<T>`, `RefCell<T>` and `OnceCell<T>` implement `Sync` when their contained type `T` implements `Sync`.
cards.explanation: Cell, RefCell and OnceCell do not implement Sync, even with a Sync inner type. Their shared mutation interfaces serve single-threaded access.
cards.misconception: A Sync inner type makes these cell containers Sync as well.

cards.statement: `Arc<T>` updates its reference counts with atomic operations, adding overhead compared with `Rc<T>`.
cards.explanation: Arc uses atomics to coordinate ownership counts across threads. Its documentation identifies their extra cost compared with ordinary memory accesses.

cards.statement: `std::thread::spawn` requires its closure to implement `Send` and satisfy `'static`.
cards.explanation: The Send bound checks that captured data is safe to transfer to the new thread. The 'static bound excludes closures borrowing shorter-lived data.

cards.statement: `JoinHandle::join` rethrows a joined thread's Rust panic in the calling thread.
cards.explanation: JoinHandle::join returns Err when the joined thread unwinds from a Rust panic. Calling code receives the panic payload as the error value.
cards.misconception: Joining a panicked thread automatically propagates its panic into the joining thread.

cards.statement: A scoped thread's closure can borrow a local `String` that outlives its `std::thread::scope` call.
cards.explanation: Scoped thread functions complete before scope returns, so their closures can borrow local data that outlives the scope.

cards.statement: Cloning an `mpsc::Sender<i32>` gives another producer access to the same channel.
cards.explanation: A Sender clone targets the original channel. Different threads can own these sender handles and send messages to the channel's receiver.

cards.statement: `sync_channel(0)` lets `send` return while its message waits in a buffer for a receiver.
cards.explanation: A zero-bound synchronous channel is a rendezvous channel. Its send waits for a matching receive instead of storing a pending message in a buffer.
cards.misconception: A zero channel bound means messages wait in an unbounded queue.

cards.statement: An `mpsc::Receiver` discards its queued messages when the final sender is dropped.
cards.explanation: Receiver::recv still returns messages queued before disconnection. Once those messages are drained and every sender is gone, it returns Err.
cards.misconception: Dropping the last sender makes buffered messages unavailable to the receiver.

cards.statement: Dropping a `MutexGuard` releases the lock that the guard holds.
cards.explanation: MutexGuard owns the active lock. Its cleanup releases that lock so another thread can acquire it.

cards.statement: A `PoisonError` from `Mutex::lock` contains the acquired guard, retrievable with `into_inner`.
cards.explanation: Mutex poisoning is advisory. PoisonError::into_inner returns the guard so code can inspect or repair the protected data.

cards.statement: Shared owners of an `Arc<Mutex<i32>>` mutate its integer while holding a mutable lock guard.
cards.explanation: Arc shares ownership of the mutex across threads. Acquiring that mutex provides exclusive mutable access to its protected integer.

cards.statement: Rust's borrow checker rejects a safe program when its mutex lock ordering leads to deadlock.
cards.explanation: Safe Rust programs can deadlock. Two threads that acquire mutexes in opposing orders can wait on each other's locks indefinitely.
cards.misconception: Compile-time borrowing checks prove that safe mutex use is free of deadlocks.

cards.statement: A type `T` implements `Sync` exactly when the reference type `&mut T` implements `Send`.
cards.explanation: Sync corresponds to &T being Send. The relevant reference is shared, because Sync governs safe sharing of a value across threads.
cards.misconception: Sync is defined by sending a mutable reference rather than a shared reference.

cards.statement: Manual `Send` and `Sync` implementations each use a safe `impl` block.
cards.explanation: Manual Send and Sync implementations require unsafe impl. The implementer takes responsibility for upholding the traits' concurrency guarantees.
cards.misconception: The automatically implemented concurrency traits also permit ordinary safe manual implementations.

source.title: Extensible Concurrency with Send and Sync
